identity.description: Jira (Atlassian's issue tracking and project management product), Jira Cloud Platform REST API
identity.identity_notes: Developer docs at developer.atlassian.com describe Jira Cloud webhooks, REST API auth, and rate limits. Confirmed as the Jira product, not a generic 'Jira' name. Sources do not describe a separate product using the Jira name in these pages.

auth.oauth_flows: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps created in the Developer console; Forge and Connect apps also referenced. Rotating refresh tokens are used.
auth.token_refresh: Rotating refresh tokens issue a new, limited life refresh token each time they are used.
auth.scopes_notes: Not researched in detail. Scope configuration was not verified from a fetched source.

access.production_restrictions: Not verified. Sources show webhooks and OAuth apps managed in admin/Connected apps context, but no app review requirement was found in fetched pages.

resources: Boards (webhook event groups only; REST resource coverage not verified)
api.rate_limits: Points-based quota measured in points per hour, reset at top of each UTC hour; HTTP 429 when exceeded. API token traffic is not affected by the new limits and remains under burst limits.
api.limitations: Basic auth with passwords is described as deprecated; API tokens are for scripts and manual calls, while apps are pointed to OAuth 2.0 or JWT. Rovo MCP uses Rovo credits for some tools. WebSocket was not verified in sources; remove if unconfirmed.

claims.value: Jira Cloud webhooks and REST API documentation from Atlassian developer portal
claims.quote: You can use Jira webhooks to notify your app or web application when certain events occur in Jira.

claims.value: Email address plus API token used as Basic auth; token generated via Atlassian account
claims.quote: Generate an API token for Jira using your Atlassian Account

claims.value: Basic authentication uses user name (email) and API token
claims.quote: Most client software provides a simple mechanism for supplying a user name (in our case, the email address) and API token

claims.value: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) app created in Developer console
claims.quote: In the Developer console, select the Create dropdown and choose OAuth 2.0 integration to create an OAuth 2.0 (3LO) app.
Rotating refresh tokens issue a new, limited life refresh token each time they are used.

claims.value: Points per hour, reset at top of UTC hour
claims.quote: All quotas are measured in points per hour and reset at the top of each UTC hour.
When any limit is exceeded, Jira returns an HTTP `429 Too Many Requests` response.

claims.value: API token traffic governed by burst limits, not new hourly quotas
claims.quote: API token-based traffic is not affected by this change, and will continue to be governed by existing burst rate limits.

claims.value: Webhooks supported; REST-registered webhooks expire after 30 days
claims.quote: Webhooks registered with the REST API expire after 30 days.

claims.value: Webhook registration methods include Jira Administration, Connect descriptors, REST API
claims.quote: To register (i.e. create) a webhook, you can use any of the following methods:

claims.value: OAuth 2.0 app webhooks secured by bearer authentication; admin webhooks signed with HMAC
claims.quote: Webhooks for OAuth 2.0 apps are secured by bearer authentication.

claims.value: Atlassian Rovo MCP Server is a cloud-hosted MCP server
claims.quote: The Atlassian Rovo MCP Server is a cloud-hosted Model Context Protocol (MCP) server

claims.value: OAuth 2.1 or API token for headless auth
claims.quote: The server initiates a secure OAuth 2.1 authorization flow (or accepts an API token for headless authentication).
New setups should use `https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp`, which exposes more tools and more products.

claims.value: Official Atlassian MCP repo owned by atlassian org, Apache-2.0
claims.quote: The official Atlassian MCP Server is a cloud-based bridge between your Atlassian Cloud site and compatible external tools.

claims.value: Community Jira MCP servers exist on npm/PyPI (not Atlassian-owned)

open_questions: Whether a free Atlassian account is sufficient to get API tokens and OAuth developer console access was not confirmed from a fetched page.
REST API resource breadth (read and write coverage across issues, projects, workflows, etc.) was not verified; the REST v3 intro page could not be fetched.
SDKs: no official Atlassian Jira SDK was verified from fetched sources.

Rovo MCP availability and GA status were only seen in search snippets (community post, localized pages with mixed Beta labels). Whether all Cloud customers get access, and Rovo plan/credit gating, need verification.
Basic auth deprecation for passwords was reported in fetch summary but not quoted verbatim.
Webhook API token registration: a community thread says API-token basic auth returned 'Only apps can access this resource' for webhook endpoints (2022); current behavior unverified.
WebSocket protocol listed in api.protocols is not verified by any fetched source; treat as unknown.
Community MCP server package details (mcp-jira-stdio, atlassian-jira-mcp, @aashari/mcp-server-atlassian-jira) came from search snippets and were not individually reviewed for maintenance or license.

assessment.approach: Wrap/benchmark vendor's official MCP server; add managed auth
rationale: Self-serve test credentials (free self serve) and a documented REST/WebSocket interface.
